sentences.text: Larsonvenator is a tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaur.
The type species of this genus is L. elegans.
The holotype skull of Nanotyrannus measures 57.2 cm from the anterior tip of the premaxilla to the posterior tip of the quadrate.
Larsonvenator was described by Sancarlo and Paul.
Nanotyrannus is based on the skull CMNH 7541, collected in 1942 by David Hosbrook Dunkle and described in 1946 by Charles W. Gilmore as a new species of Gorgosaurus.

The specimen was re-described in 1988 by Robert T. Bakker, Michael Williams, and Phil Currie, who named the genus Nanotyrannus with the type species Nanotyrannus lancensis, originally described by Gilmore in 1946.
Nanotyrannus lethaeus is a subdivision of the genus Nanotyrannus described by Zanno and Napoli in 2025.
Researchers suggest that the long hind limbs of Nanotyrannus indicate a lifestyle adapted for chasing prey, unlike the ambush style of tyrannosaurids.
Joseph Peterson and colleagues found healed puncture wounds on the skull of the Nanotyrannus holotype 'Jane', suggesting it was attacked by another juvenile Tyrannosaurus.
Bakker suggests that Nanotyrannus hunted in packs due to its weight and build.
A 2016 limb proportion analysis suggested Nanotyrannus samples had different cursoriality levels, cited as a potential difference between N. lancensis and T. rex.
Larsonvenator lived during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) age.
The type locality of Larsonvenator is the Hell Creek Formation in the United States, specifically the region of Montana.
The taxonomic status of Nanotyrannus has been a subject of intense scientific debate.
Nanotyrannus lancensis specimens are reported to have 15-16 teeth on the upper jaw and 16-18 on the lower jaw, while adult Tyrannosaurus rex have 11-12 upper and 12-14 lower teeth.
Carr hypothesized that Nanotyrannus lancensis is a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex based on a decrease in tooth count during growth observed in Gorgosaurus libratus.
Tsujihi and colleagues noted that tooth count varies individually in Tyrannosaurus and Gorgosaurus regardless of age, suggesting it may not indicate distinct species.
